title: Branching strategies and trunk-based development
description: Master branching strategies from Git Flow to trunk-based development. Learn when to use each model, how feature flags enable continuous delivery, and how senior engineers choose the right approach for their team and codebase.

data.text: **Branching strategies and trunk-based development** form the foundation of how teams collaborate on code. Choosing the right strategy affects deployment frequency, code review load, merge conflict rates, and overall team velocity. Senior engineers must understand the trade-offs between isolation and integration, and know how to adapt their approach to the team's maturity, release cadence, and risk tolerance.
Why Branching Strategy Matters

Branching strategy is not just a Git convention—it is a team coordination protocol. A poor strategy leads to long-lived branches, painful merge conflicts, delayed feedback, and production incidents from untested integrations. A well-chosen strategy enables continuous integration, fast deployment, and high developer confidence.

data.title: The Trunk-Based Development Advantage
data.text: Trunk-based development (TBD) is the strategy used by Google, Facebook, and Microsoft. Teams commit directly to main or use short-lived feature branches (under one day). Feature flags decouple deployment from release, allowing incomplete code to ship safely.
Git Flow: The Classic Model

Git Flow, popularized by Vincent Driessen in 2010, defines five branch types with distinct lifetimes and purposes: main (production), develop (integration), feature branches, release branches, and hotfix branches. It works well for scheduled release cycles but creates integration debt when feature branches live for weeks.

data.title: Git Flow Branch Types
items: **main** — Contains production-ready code. Every commit is a release. Tags mark versions.
**develop** — Integration branch for the next release. Feature branches merge here.
**feature/\*** — Branched from develop. Merged back into develop via pull request. Lifetime: days to weeks.
**release/\*** — Branched from develop when the release is ready. Only bug fixes merge here. Merged into main and develop.
**hotfix/\*** — Branched from main for urgent production fixes. Merged into main and develop.

data.title: Git Flow Lifecycle Example
data.content: A feature branch lifecycle in Git Flow
data.code:
# Start a new feature
git checkout develop
git checkout -b feature/user-authentication

# Work on the feature...
git add .
git commit -m "feat(auth): add OAuth2 login flow"

# Finish the feature (merge back to develop)
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff feature/user-authentication

# When ready to release, create a release branch
git checkout -b release/v2.1.0

# After QA, merge to main and tag
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff release/v2.1.0
git tag -a v2.1.0 -m "Release v2.1.0"

# Also merge back to develop
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff release/v2.1.0

data.title: Git Flow Drawbacks
data.text: Long-lived feature branches diverge significantly from develop. When finally merged, conflicts are large and risky. Integration happens late, not continuously. The develop branch becomes a merge bottleneck. Many teams have moved away from Git Flow for these reasons.
GitHub Flow: Simpler Continuous Delivery

GitHub Flow, created by GitHub, is simpler: main is always deployable, and any change (feature, fix, experiment) lives in a short-lived topic branch. You create a branch from main, add commits, open a pull request, and merge after review and CI pass. There is no develop branch. This model suits teams deploying continuously.

data.title: GitHub Flow Principles
items: **Main is always deployable** — The main branch reflects the current production state or can be deployed immediately.
**Branch for everything** — No matter the change size, create a descriptive branch.
**Merge via pull request** — Code review and CI must pass before merging.
**Deploy often** — Merge to main triggers deployment. Production is the only long-lived branch.

data.title: GitHub Flow Daily Workflow
data.content: Typical GitHub Flow commands for a small bug fix
data.code:
# Start from up-to-date main
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Create a descriptive branch
git checkout -b fix/header-overflow-mobile

# Make changes, commit, and push
git add src/components/Header.tsx
git commit -m "fix(header): prevent overflow on mobile viewports"
git push -u origin fix/header-overflow-mobile

# Open a PR on GitHub. After review and CI pass:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge --ff-only fix/header-overflow-mobile
git push origin main

data.text: Trunk-Based Development (TBD)

Trunk-based development takes GitHub Flow further: developers integrate their work into the trunk (main) at least once per day. Long-lived branches are forbidden or heavily discouraged. Feature flags wrap incomplete work so it does not affect users. This approach maximizes integration frequency and minimizes merge conflicts.

data.title: TBD Practices
items: **Short-lived branches** — Feature branches last hours, not days. Merge to main at least daily.
**Feature flags** — Incomplete features are hidden behind flags. Flag off = feature invisible to users.
**Branch by abstraction** — Instead of branching, introduce an abstraction layer, implement the new behavior behind it, then switch over.
**Pair programming / mob programming** — Reduces branch proliferation by having two developers work on the same trunk commit.
**Continuous integration** — Every commit to main is built and tested automatically.

data.title: Feature Flag Pattern in Code
data.content: Wrapping a new feature behind a flag for trunk-based development

data.title: Branch by Abstraction
data.text: When a feature requires multiple weeks but you want to avoid long-lived branches, use branch by abstraction. Introduce an interface or abstract class, implement the new logic alongside the old, then gradually route traffic. This technique is especially valuable for database migrations or large refactors.
Feature Flags: The Enabler of TBD

Feature flags (also called feature toggles) are the technical mechanism that makes trunk-based development practical. They allow you to merge incomplete code to main without exposing it to users. Flags can be boolean, percentage-based (canary releases), or user-targeted.

data.title: Feature Flag Types
rows: Gradual rollout to subset of users
Enable for specific users or segments
Based on user role or plan
Kill switches for performance or cost

Your current Git Flow has feature branches living 2-3 weeks. Design a migration plan from Git Flow to trunk-based development with feature flags.

data.text: Release Branch Strategies

Even in trunk-based development, teams sometimes need a dedicated release branch. This is common when preparing a versioned release while development continues on main. The release branch is created from main, receives only bug fixes, and is merged back after the release.

data.title: Release Branch Workflow
items: Create release branch from main when the release criteria are met
Only bug fixes merge to the release branch; new features go to main
Run final QA and performance tests on the release branch
Tag the release commit and deploy from the branch
Merge the release branch back to main to capture any bug fixes
Delete the release branch after successful deployment

data.title: Release Branch Commands
data.content: Creating and managing a release branch
data.code:
# Create release branch from main
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b release/v3.0.0

# Bug fix on release branch
git commit -m "fix(release): patch payment timeout on v3.0.0"

# Tag and deploy
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff release/v3.0.0
git tag -a v3.0.0 -m "v3.0.0"
git push origin v3.0.0

# Also merge back to develop if it exists
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff release/v3.0.0

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Trunk-based development reduces merge conflicts and increases deployment frequency
Feature flags enable incomplete code to ship safely to main
GitHub Flow is simpler than Git Flow and suits continuous delivery teams
Release branches are for final bug fixing before a versioned deployment
The best strategy depends on team maturity, release cadence, and risk tolerance
data.takeaway: Senior engineers choose branching strategies based on team context, not dogma. The goal is fast, safe integration.

data.text: Understanding Branch Lifetimes

Every branch has a lifetime. The key metric is 'branch age'—how long a branch exists before merging. Research by DORA and Accelerate shows that teams with short-lived branches (under one day) have higher deployment frequency and lower change failure rates.

data.title: Branch Lifetime Guidelines
items: **Hours**: Ideal for trunk-based development. The branch contains one logical change.
**1 day**: Acceptable maximum for feature branches in high-velocity teams.
**3-5 days**: Warning zone. Rebase onto main daily to minimize conflicts.
**1+ week**: Danger zone. The branch will have significant divergence. Consider splitting the work.
**2+ weeks**: Critical. Almost guaranteed merge conflicts and integration debt. Never allow this.

data.title: The Merge Conflict Tax
data.text: Every day a branch lives, it accrues 'integration debt.' A branch that is 2 weeks old may have hundreds of conflicting lines when finally merged. This tax is paid in developer hours, not just Git operations. Short-lived branches minimize this cost.
Git Flow Deep Dive

Vincent Driessen's Git Flow was the dominant model for a decade. It defines five branch types with strict rules about what merges where and when. Understanding Git Flow is still valuable because you will encounter it in enterprise and legacy projects, and it provides a clear mental model for release management.

data.title: Git Flow Directory Structure
data.content: Visual representation of Git Flow branches
data.code:
main (production)
  |
  |--- release/v2.0 (tagged, then merged back)
  |
develop (integration branch)
  |
  |--- feature/auth
  |--- feature/dashboard
  |--- release/v1.9 (branched from develop)
  |
  |--- hotfix/v1.9.1 (branched from main)

Each branch has a distinct purpose and merge destination.

data.text: When Git Flow Makes Sense

Git Flow is appropriate when your team has scheduled releases (e.g., bi-weekly or monthly), needs a dedicated stabilization period, and manages multiple production versions simultaneously. It provides a clear separation between development and release code.

items: Scheduled release cycles with QA periods
Need to support multiple production versions
Strict change management processes (common in regulated industries)
Large teams with specialized release engineering
Mobile apps where app store review adds latency

data.text: When Git Flow Causes Pain

The problems with Git Flow emerge when feature branches live too long. The develop branch becomes a 'merge soup' of divergent code. Integration happens late, not continuously. Teams spend more time resolving conflicts than building features.

data.title: The Git Flow Trap
data.text: If your team uses Git Flow and feature branches live for more than 3 days, you are experiencing integration debt. Consider shortening branch lifetimes, adding CI gating on develop, or migrating to trunk-based development with feature flags.
GitHub Flow Deep Dive

GitHub Flow removes the develop branch entirely. Main is always deployable. Every change, regardless of size, gets its own branch and pull request. This simplicity is powerful but requires discipline: every commit to main must be production-ready.

data.title: GitHub Flow Rules
items: Any change gets a branch from main
Branch names should be descriptive: fix/login-error, feat/dark-mode
Open a pull request as soon as the branch is pushed
CI must pass before review
At least one approval required for merge
Merge via 'Squash and merge' or 'Rebase and merge' to keep main linear
Delete the branch after merge

data.title: Squash Merge in GitHub Flow
data.content: Keeping main linear with squash merges
data.code:
# On the feature branch, you have 5 commits:
# feat: add user model
# feat: add user service
# fix: correct email validation
# refactor: extract constants
# chore: update tests

# Squash merge to main creates ONE commit on main:
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature/user-profile
git commit -m "feat(users): add user profile with email validation"

git push origin main

# Result: main has a single clean commit per logical change.

data.title: Squash vs Rebase vs Merge Commit
data.text: Squash merge collapses all branch commits into one. Rebase and merge replays each commit individually. Merge commit preserves the branch topology. Choose based on whether you want a clean linear history (squash/rebase) or full provenance (merge commit).
Trunk-Based Development Deep Dive

Trunk-based development is the gold standard for high-performance engineering organizations. The core principle is simple: integrate to main at least once per day. This requires feature flags for incomplete work, automated testing to catch regressions instantly, and a culture that values integration over isolation.

data.title: TBD Implementation Checklist
items: Main branch is always deployable
Developers integrate to main at least daily
Feature branches are under 1 day old when merged
All commits to main pass CI (build, test, lint)
Feature flags protect incomplete work from users
Pair programming or mob programming reduces individual branch divergence
Monitoring and feature flag metrics enable safe rollbacks

data.title: Trunk-Based Daily Workflow
data.content: A senior engineer's daily workflow with trunk-based development
data.code:
# Morning: pull latest main
git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Create a small feature branch (max 1 day of work)
git checkout -b feat/cache-invalidation

# Work in small commits, integrating frequently:
# - Commit 1: add cache interface
# - Commit 2: implement Redis cache
# - Commit 3: add cache invalidation logic
# - Commit 4: add tests

# Before lunch, rebase onto main and push
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push -u origin feat/cache-invalidation --force-with-lease

# Open PR. After CI and review, merge:
# (squash merge on GitHub)

# Feature is behind a flag. Deploy to production safely.

data.title: Force With Lease
data.text: Always use --force-with-lease instead of --force when rewriting public branch history. It fails if the remote branch has new commits you do not have locally, preventing accidental overwrites of your teammates' work.
Feature Flags Deep Dive

Feature flags are the backbone of trunk-based development. They allow incomplete or risky code to exist on main without affecting users. A well-designed flag system supports rollout percentages, targeted audiences, and kill switches for emergency rollbacks.

data.title: Feature Flag Best Practices
items: Use descriptive flag names: NEW_CHECKOUT_FLOW, not flag1
Set a removal date for every flag—flags are temporary, not permanent
Keep flag logic simple; complex branching logic inside flags becomes its own maintenance burden
Test both flag-on and flag-off states
Monitor flag metrics: adoption rate, error rate, latency impact
Clean up flags after full rollout to prevent flag sprawl
Use environment variables for simple boolean flags
Use a feature flag service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash) for complex targeting

data.title: Feature Flag Cleanup Workflow
data.content: Removing a feature flag after full rollout

data.text: Branch by Abstraction

Branch by abstraction is a technique for making large-scale changes without long-lived branches. Instead of creating a feature branch that lives for weeks, you introduce an abstraction layer in small, mergeable increments. The old and new implementations coexist until you are ready to switch over.

data.title: Branch by Abstraction Steps
items: Identify the code to change (e.g., a database repository)
Introduce an interface or abstract class around the existing code
Implement the new behavior behind the same interface
Use a feature flag or configuration to switch between implementations
Gradually route traffic to the new implementation
Remove the old implementation and the abstraction layer

data.title: Branch by Abstraction: Database Migration
data.content: Migrating from MongoDB to PostgreSQL without a long-lived branch

data.title: Strangler Fig Pattern
data.text: Branch by abstraction is related to the Strangler Fig pattern. Instead of replacing a monolith all at once, you incrementally intercept requests and route them to the new system. Both patterns enable large changes in small, safe increments.
Pair Programming and Mob Programming

Pair programming is a powerful complement to trunk-based development. When two developers work on the same feature together, they naturally produce fewer, larger commits that integrate cleanly to main. Mob programming extends this to the whole team for complex architectural changes.

data.title: Pair Programming Benefits for TBD
items: Reduces individual branch divergence—two people on one branch means fewer branches overall
Increases code quality through real-time review
Shares knowledge across the team, reducing bus factor
Produces more thoughtful commit messages when done together
Enables faster onboarding of junior developers

data.text: Comparing Branching Strategies

items.title: Git Flow
cons: Complex merge rules are hard to enforce
items.bestFor: Scheduled releases, regulated industries, multiple supported versions

items.title: GitHub Flow
cons: Can feel chaotic for large teams
items.bestFor: Continuous delivery teams, SaaS products, small to medium teams

items.title: Trunk-Based Development
items.bestFor: High-velocity teams, microservices, CI/CD mature organizations

data.text: Choosing the Right Strategy

No branching strategy is universally best. The right choice depends on your team's release cadence, codebase size, regulatory requirements, and engineering culture. A common mistake is choosing a strategy for its popularity rather than its fit.

data.title: Decision Framework
items: If you deploy continuously and have strong CI: choose Trunk-Based Development
If you deploy weekly with a QA freeze: choose GitHub Flow with release branches
If you have monthly releases and support multiple versions: choose Git Flow or a simplified variant
If you are a small team (1-5 developers): GitHub Flow or Trunk-Based keeps overhead low
If you are regulated (medical, finance): Git Flow provides audit trails and release isolation
If your codebase is a monolith with shared state: Trunk-Based with feature flags reduces integration risk

data.text: Common Pitfalls and Anti-Patterns
Even with a well-chosen strategy, teams fall into anti-patterns that erode the benefits. Recognizing these patterns is the first step to correcting them.

data.title: Branching Anti-Patterns
items: **The Mega-Feature Branch**: A branch that lives for weeks and contains hundreds of commits. Fix: Split into smaller, mergeable increments.
**The Zombie Branch**: A feature branch that was abandoned but never deleted. Fix: Regular branch cleanup; set a 7-day expiry policy.
**The Develop Drift**: In Git Flow, develop diverges so far from main that the next release is a nightmare. Fix: Merge main into develop weekly.
**Flag Sprawl**: Hundreds of feature flags never cleaned up. Fix: Assign an owner and removal date to every flag.
**Commit Then Merge**: Developers commit directly to main without PR review. Fix: Enforce branch protection rules on main.
**Rebase After Merge**: Rewriting history on a branch after it has been merged. Fix: Treat merged branches as immutable.

data.title: Detecting Anti-Patterns with Git
data.content: Finding zombie branches and stale feature branches
data.code:
# List all branches sorted by last commit date
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate refs/heads/

# Find branches not updated in 30 days (zombie branches)
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(committerdate:relative)' refs/heads/ | \
  awk '$2 ~ /weeks|months/ {print $0}'

# Count open PRs by author (GitHub CLI)
gh pr list --state open --json author,createdAt | \
  jq 'group_by(.author.login) | map({author: .[0].author.login, count: length})'

data.title: Branch Protection Rules
data.text: Configure branch protection on main: require PR reviews, require CI pass, disallow force pushes, and require status checks. This prevents accidental direct commits and ensures every change is reviewed and tested.

data.text: Real-World Case Studies

Studying how successful companies implement branching strategies provides concrete evidence for the trade-offs discussed. Google, GitHub, and Shopify represent different points on the strategy spectrum.

data.title: Company Case Studies
items: **Google**: Uses a single trunk with Piper (their custom source control). Code is reviewed before commit. No long-lived branches. Feature flags are mandatory for user-facing changes.
**GitHub**: Created GitHub Flow specifically for their continuous deployment model. Every push to main triggers a deploy to production.
**Shopify**: Uses trunk-based development with feature flags. They deploy hundreds of times per day. Long-lived branches are forbidden.
**Microsoft (Windows)**: Uses Git Flow with a modified 'master' branch because Windows releases on a 6-month cycle and needs a stabilization period.
**Netflix**: Uses trunk-based development with canary releases. Feature flags control rollout percentages from 1% to 100%.

data.text: Setting Up Trunk-Based Development
Transitioning from Git Flow or GitHub Flow to trunk-based development requires changes to your tooling, culture, and processes. Here is a step-by-step migration plan.

data.title: TBD Migration Steps
items: Audit current feature branch lifetimes. If average lifetime > 3 days, start here.
Choose a pilot feature to implement with a feature flag. Pick something low-risk.
Set up a feature flag service or use environment variables for boolean flags.
Configure CI to run on every push to main with a 10-minute maximum feedback loop.
Set branch protection on main: require PR, require CI, no force pushes.
Train the team on short-lived branches. Target: max 1 day lifetime.
Establish a 'trunk health' metric: how often does main pass CI? Target: >95%.
Add monitoring to track feature flag adoption and error rates.
After 4 weeks, review deployment frequency and change failure rate. Adjust as needed.

data.text: CI/CD Integration with Branching Strategies

Branching strategy and CI/CD pipeline are deeply connected. The pipeline must match the branching model: fast feedback for trunk-based, thorough testing for release branches, and gated deployments for production branches.

data.title: CI/CD Pipeline by Strategy
rows: Full test suite + deploy to staging
Full test suite + deploy to staging

data.title: CI Feedback Loop
data.text: The goal is a feedback loop under 10 minutes from commit to CI result. If your pipeline takes longer, developers will context-switch and branch divergence will increase. Invest in test parallelization and caching.
Release Branch Management

Release branches are a specialized branch type used to prepare a production release. They exist between the completion of feature development and the actual deployment. During this window, only bug fixes merge to the release branch; new features continue on develop or main.

data.title: Release Branch Lifecycle
items: Create release branch from develop (Git Flow) or main when release criteria are met
Freeze feature development on the release branch
Apply only bug fixes and documentation updates
Run regression tests, performance tests, and security scans
Create a release candidate (RC) and deploy to staging
After QA approval, tag the release and deploy to production
Merge the release branch back to develop and main
Delete the release branch

data.title: Release Branch Script
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
# release.sh - Create and manage a release branch
VERSION=$1

if [ -z "$VERSION" ]; then
  echo "Usage: ./release.sh v1.2.3"
  exit 1
fi

git checkout develop
git pull origin develop
git checkout -b release/$VERSION

echo "Release branch 'release/$VERSION' created."
echo "Push and open a PR for QA testing:"
echo "  git push -u origin release/$VERSION"

data.text: Hotfix Branches

Hotfix branches handle urgent production issues. They are created from the production tag (or main), fixed, and merged back to both main and develop. This ensures the fix is not lost when the next release branches off develop.

data.title: Hotfix Best Practices
items: Create from the tagged production commit, not main or develop
Use the smallest possible fix—do not refactor or add features
Cherry-pick the fix to any active release branches
Merge to main (tag new patch version) and develop
Deploy the hotfix immediately after merge
Communicate the fix to stakeholders with a timeline

data.text: Team Conventions and Documentation
A branching strategy is only effective if the entire team follows it. Document the conventions, automate enforcement where possible, and revisit the strategy quarterly as the team and product evolve.

items.text: Written branching strategy document in the team wiki
items.hint: Include diagrams, branch naming, and merge rules

items.text: Branch naming conventions enforced via git hooks or CI
PR templates that require description, testing steps, and screenshots
CODEOWNERS file for automatic review assignment
Branch protection rules configured on main and develop
items.hint: Require reviews, CI pass, no force push

data.text: Measuring Branching Strategy Success

DORA metrics (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, MTTR) are the standard for measuring DevOps performance. Use them to evaluate whether your branching strategy is helping or hurting.

data.title: Exercise: DORA Metrics Audit
data.description: Calculate your team's current DORA metrics and map them to your branching strategy. Identify one bottleneck caused by your current branching model and propose a concrete improvement.
steps: Measure average PR merge time from creation
Track percentage of deployments that cause incidents
Measure mean time to recovery from incidents
Identify which metric is worst and trace it to a branching cause
data.expectedOutcome: A metrics dashboard with one prioritized improvement backed by data.

data.text: Migrating Between Strategies
Changing branching strategies mid-project is risky but sometimes necessary. A phased migration minimizes disruption. Start with a pilot team or module, document the new process, and gradually expand.

data.title: Migration Playbook
items: Week 1-2: Document current pain points and define target strategy
Week 3-4: Pilot with one team or one product area
Week 5-6: Gather feedback, adjust strategy, fix tooling gaps
Week 7-8: Roll out to second team with lessons learned
Month 3: Full rollout with dedicated support channel
Ongoing: Quarterly review of strategy effectiveness

data.title: The Strangler Fig Migration
data.text: When migrating strategies, do not rewrite history. Instead, apply the new strategy going forward. Old branches can follow the old rules until they are merged. This avoids disrupting in-flight work.
Advanced Topics
For large organizations, additional considerations include cross-repo branching strategies, monorepo tooling, and governance models for open source projects.

data.title: Advanced Considerations
items: **Monorepos**: Trunk-based with selective deployment. Tools like Nx or Bazel handle build/test scoping.
**Open source projects**: Maintain a stable main branch; contributors use PRs with rebase. No long-lived branches from maintainers.
**Git submodules and subtrees**: Branching strategies must account for coupled repositories.
**Cross-functional teams**: Frontend, backend, and DevOps may have different branch lifetimes. Align on integration points.
**Regulatory compliance**: Git Flow provides better audit trails for changes over time.

items.question: Can I mix Git Flow and trunk-based development?
items.answer: Yes. Many teams use Git Flow for release management but require daily integration to develop or main. The key is enforcing a maximum branch lifetime regardless of the overall strategy.

items.question: Do feature flags add complexity?
items.answer: Yes, but the complexity is manageable. Start with simple boolean flags in environment variables. Only adopt a flag service when you need targeting, analytics, or kill switches.

items.question: What if my team is not ready for trunk-based development?
items.answer: Start with GitHub Flow. It is simpler than Git Flow and encourages shorter branches. Add feature flags and stricter CI as the team matures. Progress, not perfection.

items.question: How do I handle database migrations in trunk-based development?
items.answer: Use expand-contract migrators: expand the schema to support both old and new code, deploy, contract the old schema. This lets you ship database changes in small, reversible steps.

items.question: Should I rebase feature branches before merging?
items.answer: Yes, rebasing onto main before merge reduces merge commits and keeps history linear. Use --force-with-lease to avoid overwriting teammates' work. Never rebase a branch that others are basing work on.

data.title: Senior Engineer Takeaways
points: Choose your branching strategy based on team context, not blog popularity
Short-lived branches are the single most impactful change for merge health
Feature flags enable trunk-based development by decoupling deploy from release
Release branches are for stabilization, not feature development
Measure success with DORA metrics, not branch count
data.takeaway: A branching strategy is a team coordination tool, not a religion. Adapt it to your context and evolve it as your team grows.
